lead: Proportional navigation (PN) is a homing law that commands missile acceleration proportional to the rate at which the line of sight rotates. Zero line-of-sight rate means the missile is on a collision course. PN needs only angle measurements from a seeker, not target range or target speed. It is used in air-to-air, surface-to-air and anti-ship missiles and in guided bombs. This chapter gives the base law, the main variants, and how each behaves against a target that manoeuvres.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for guidance-law families and Chapter 6.4 for line-of-sight geometry and why pursuit and CLOS leave a LOS rate.

blocks.text: Draw the missile M and target T. The line joining them is the line of sight (LOS). The angle λ is the LOS direction from a fixed reference. The LOS rate λ̇ = dλ/dt is how fast that line rotates, in rad/s. Range R is the distance M to T. Closing velocity V<sub>c</sub> = −dR/dt is positive when the range shrinks, in m/s. A seeker measures λ directly; V<sub>c</sub> may come from a radar or from an estimate.

If λ̇ = 0 while R decreases, the LOS keeps one direction. Missile and target stay on a straight line, so a hit follows. This is a collision course: constant bearing, decreasing range. Any nonzero λ̇ means the missile is sliding off that line. The seeker measures λ and λ̇; PN uses λ̇ as its error signal. The guidance computer is inside the missile because this is homing guidance, as Chapter 6.3 explains.

sections.h3: Base law: a = N Vc λ̇

blocks.where: a is the commanded acceleration perpendicular to the LOS, in m/s²; N is the effective navigation ratio, dimensionless; V<sub>c</sub> is closing velocity in m/s; λ̇ is LOS rate in rad/s.

blocks.text: The command is proportional to the rotation rate. If the LOS rotates faster, the missile turns harder. The sign of λ̇ sets the direction. At λ̇ = 0 the command is zero, so the missile does not turn away from a collision course.

Why this drives λ̇ to zero: a turn perpendicular to the LOS changes the missile velocity direction so as to reduce LOS rotation. That is negative feedback. The gain N sets how strongly the loop reacts. Typical N is 3 to 5. Below about 2 the loop can fail to converge; above 5 the response is fast but sensitive to seeker noise and fin saturation. N carries no units, so the units of a come from V<sub>c</sub> λ̇: (m/s)(1/s) = m/s².
Use rad/s, not deg/s. One degree per second equals π/180 = 0.01745 rad/s. A seeker that reports 1 °/s has λ̇ = 0.01745 rad/s.

blocks.text: V<sub>m</sub> is missile speed in m/s; a<sub>T⊥</sub> is the component of target acceleration normal to the LOS, in m/s²; b is a fixed bias acceleration, in m/s². Pure PN (PPN) is the base law. True PN (TPN) does not change the missile speed, only its direction. When V<sub>c</sub> is close to V<sub>m</sub> the two commands are close; in a fast head-on engagement V<sub>c</sub> can be much larger, so PPN asks for a larger acceleration.

Augmented PN (APN) adds half of N times the target acceleration normal to the LOS. That term cancels a steady target turn instead of waiting for it to show up as LOS rate. Biased PN (BPN) adds a constant bias b, used to shape the path or add lead. Generalised PN (GPN) is the general form; set b = 0 and it becomes APN. Ideal PN (IPN) keeps the exact geometry without small-angle approximations and is used as a benchmark for what PPN loses.

sections.h3: Manoeuvring targets and the choice of N

blocks.text: Against a non-manoeuvring target, PPN drives λ̇ near zero with bounded acceleration. Miss distance is small if N is in the usual range and the seeker and fins are fast enough. The missile does not need target range, only closing speed.

Against a manoeuvring target, PPN leaves a steady-state miss unless N is large. The target's turn creates LOS rotation; PPN reacts only after λ̇ appears, so it always lags. APN adds (N/2) a<sub>T⊥</sub>, which is nonzero even when λ̇ is zero, so the command anticipates the target turn.

Higher N lowers miss distance but raises acceleration demand at launch and makes the missile more sensitive to seeker noise, target glint and fin saturation. Lower N is gentler but slower. The usual design range is 3 to 5. The fin servos and airframe must produce the commanded acceleration; see Chapter 6.6.

examples.question: An air-to-air missile closes on a target at V<sub>c</sub> = 900 m/s. The missile speed is V<sub>m</sub> = 600 m/s. The seeker measures a LOS rate of 0.02 rad/s. The navigation ratio is N = 4. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the PPN acceleration and the TPN acceleration, each in m/s² and in g. State the direction of each.
steps: Write the PPN law: a<sub>PPN</sub> = N V<sub>c</sub> λ̇.
The PPN acceleration is perpendicular to the LOS.
Write the TPN law: a<sub>TPN</sub> = N V<sub>m</sub> λ̇.
The TPN acceleration is perpendicular to the missile velocity.
examples.answer: PPN commands 72 m/s² (7.3 g) perpendicular to the LOS; TPN commands 48 m/s² (4.9 g) perpendicular to the missile velocity.
examples.check:
Vc = 900.0
Vm = 600.0
lam_dot = 0.02
N = 4.0
g = 9.81

a_ppn = N * Vc * lam_dot
a_tpn = N * Vm * lam_dot

print(round(a_ppn, 1))
print(round(a_tpn, 1))
print(round(a_ppn / g, 1))
print(round(a_tpn / g, 1))

traps: Feeding λ̇ in degrees per second instead of rad/s: the command comes out 57.3 times too large.
Putting V<sub>m</sub> into the PPN formula or V<sub>c</sub> into the TPN formula. PPN uses closing speed; TPN uses missile speed.
Thinking N has units or that a larger N is always better. N is dimensionless, usually 3 to 5; larger N raises noise sensitivity and fin saturation.
Dropping the sign of λ̇. The sign sets the turn direction, and a sign error doubles the miss instead of removing it.
Adding the whole target acceleration in APN instead of (N/2) times its component normal to the LOS.

quiz.q: What does a line-of-sight rate of zero mean for a missile closing on a target?
quiz.a: The LOS direction is not rotating; the missile is on a collision course, so it will hit if the range keeps shrinking.

quiz.q: Why does the PPN command fall to zero when the LOS rate is zero?
quiz.a: The command is a = N Vc λ̇, so it is proportional to λ̇. At λ̇ = 0 the product is zero; the missile needs no further turn to stay on the collision course.

quiz.q: A missile has V<sub>c</sub> = 1000 m/s, N = 4 and λ̇ = 0.01 rad/s. Find the PPN acceleration.
For TPN, V<sub>m</sub> = 500 m/s, N = 3 and λ̇ = 0.03 rad/s. Find the acceleration.
quiz.a: a = N Vm λ̇ = 3 × 500 × 0.03 = 45 m/s² perpendicular to the missile velocity.

quiz.q: Why does APN do better than PPN against a target that turns steadily?
quiz.a: PPN waits for the target turn to create LOS rate, so it lags and leaves a steady-state miss. APN adds (N/2) a_T⊥, which is present even at zero LOS rate, so it cancels the target's normal acceleration and removes that lag.

quiz.q: What happens when N is raised from 3 to 6?
quiz.a: Miss distance against a manoeuvring target falls, but the commanded acceleration rises, the missile reacts more strongly to seeker noise and glint, and the fins may saturate. The loop can also become less stable.

quiz.q: State the direction of the acceleration in PPN and in TPN.
quiz.a: PPN acceleration is perpendicular to the LOS; TPN acceleration is perpendicular to the missile velocity vector.

quiz.q: A seeker gives λ̇ = 0.5 °/s. Convert it to rad/s and find the PPN command for N = 4 and V<sub>c</sub> = 800 m/s.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production missiles combine PN with Kalman filters that estimate LOS rate from noisy seeker angles, and with guidance-integrator loops that shape the command before the fins see it. Newer work studies PN against high-speed manoeuvring targets, dual-seeker guidance and impact-angle control. Search "augmented proportional navigation", "guidance law design" and "missile autopilot" to go further.
